title: Design a class that, given a value K and an initial list of numbers, returns the Kth largest number each time a new number is added to the stream. Explain how a min-heap of size K supports this efficiently.
shortTitle: Kth Largest Number in a Stream (Maintain the Kth Largest as Numbers Arrive)
keyPoints: Maintain a min-heap of size K containing the K largest numbers; its root is the Kth largest at all times
Each add operation offers a number and trims the heap back to K, costing O(log K) per add
Numbers too small to be in the top K get polled immediately and never affect the answer
The constructor seeds the initial numbers through the same add method to avoid duplicated logic
Memory stays at O(K) regardless of how many numbers stream in, which is the key scalability property
This is LeetCode 703 and a classic Top K Elements streaming design problem
For a single query on static data, quickselect at O(n) average is cheaper than streaming

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a min-heap of size K of the largest numbers; its root is always the Kth largest as the stream grows.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Kth Largest in a Stream** – a design problem where a class must report the Kth largest number seen so far each time a new number arrives.
- **Min-heap of size K** – holds the K largest numbers; its root is the smallest of those K, which is the Kth largest overall.
- **Add operation** – offer the number, trim the heap to size K by polling the root if it grew, and return the root as the current Kth largest.
- **Constructor** – seeds the initial numbers through the same add path so the heap self-limits to K.
- **Complexity** – O(log K) per add, O(K) space regardless of stream length.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the operations dashboard continuously watches incoming transaction amounts and must always display the Kth largest amount so far as a threshold alert. Rajesh keeps a small bucket of the K largest amounts seen so far, with the smallest of those K on top. Each new amount either replaces the top if it is large enough to enter the top K, or gets discarded. The top of the bucket is always the Kth largest, and the bucket never grows beyond K entries no matter how long the stream runs.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Kth Largest in a Stream (K=3)

  Stream: 400, 500, 800, 200, 300, 900, 100

  ┌──────────┐
  │ Min-Heap  │  (bounded to size K=3)
  │ root = Kth│
  │ largest   │
  └──────────┘

  After 400:   Heap [400]             root=400
  After 500:   Heap [400,500]         root=400
  After 800:   Heap [400,500,800]     root=400  (Kth=400)
  After 200:   Heap [400,500,800]     root=400  (200 evicted)
  After 300:   Heap [400,500,800]     root=400  (300 evicted)
  After 900:   Heap [500,800,900]     root=500  (400 evicted)
  After 100:   Heap [500,800,900]     root=500  (100 evicted)

  Root of min-heap of size K = Kth largest at all times
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Largest in a Stream is a stateful design problem from the Top K Elements family. The structure you maintain is a min-heap bounded to size K that always contains the K largest numbers seen so far. Because it is a min-heap, its root is the smallest of those K, which is exactly the Kth largest overall, so answering a query is just reading the root.

When a new number arrives you offer it into the heap and then, if the heap now holds more than K elements, you poll the root to trim it back to K. A number too small to belong in the top K gets polled straight back out and never affects the answer, while a large enough number pushes the old Kth largest out and the new root becomes the updated Kth largest. Seeding the initial numbers through the same add method keeps the logic in one place.

The key scalability property is that the heap holds exactly K entries no matter how long the stream runs, so memory is fixed and each update costs only O(log K). This is what makes it practical for real-time monitoring systems where millions of events flow through.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this for a live threshold alert that always reported the Kth largest transaction amount on a never-ending stream, flagging unusually large or suspiciously quiet activity. The fixed memory footprint meant the dashboard could run indefinitely without growing.

Remember one sentence: for the Kth largest in a stream, keep a min-heap of size K and the root always holds the answer.
